title: Judging and Grading every Fitness Channel (I: Greg Doucette, AlphaDestiny, Ryan Humiston...)
summary: NH introduces a 200-point grading system (17 criteria plus 3 bonuses, 10 points each) and grades six big fitness channels: AlphaDestiny 146, Greg Doucette 106.5, Buff Dudes, Sean Nalewanyj 148.5, Omar Isuf 143 and Ryan Humiston 100. Along the way he gives his views on integrity, black-pilling, parasocial fandoms, science misuse, clickbait and content recycling in fitness YouTube.
claims: Fitness channels can be graded semi-objectively on 17 criteria (programming, experience, integrity, usefulness, character, dogmatism, originality, black pill, humor, parasocial, empathy, god complex, production, science, clickbait, content recycling, conciseness) plus 3 bonuses (seniority, not selling supplements, physique), each 0-10, for 200 points max
A fitness youtuber's character is almost as important as their content because the content is directly linked to who they are; bad people tend to make bad content
Experience means how long someone has lifted and what they did in that time, not how their physique looks
Black-pilling, telling people nothing is possible and projecting one's own despair onto viewers, is a major fault in a fitness creator
Big creators' heads inflate as subscribers grow; many confuse their own subjectivity with objectivity and cannot take criticism

Science in fitness content should serve the audience and underline training principles, not be used to bully others, win arguments or sell products; a good creator balances anecdotal and empirical evidence

Content recycling, the same theme six months later with a new title and thumbnail, is very common in fitness YouTube; since fitness is finite, some recycling is unavoidable unless you branch out as NH did
Wasting a viewer's time with no payback is an insult; conciseness matters

AlphaDestiny scored 146/200: programming 8.5 (credits Westside etc.), integrity 9, usefulness 9 even for advanced lifters, black pill 10, no supplements; weaker on humor, content recycling (many near-identical overhead press videos) and cherry-picked science
AlphaDestiny's most original period (his Italian phase) was also when he gave his worst advice
Good fitness advice tends to be boring and bland, because what works is not revolutionary
It takes some dogmatism to go far on YouTube because audiences dislike creators who keep changing their minds
Citing science only when it corroborates what you already think is dogmatism, and nearly every fitness youtuber does it

Greg Doucette scored 106.5/200: integrity 0 (self-described sellout who scams and does damage control), black pill 1, clickbait 0, supplements 0, parasocial 2; usefulness 8 for novices and physique 9.5, but enhanced
Greg dumbs programming down so much for novices that the terms lose meaning and he gets lost himself; unclear terminology is the problem
NH does not mark people down for taking drugs, but years on drugs tend to make people give bad advice to naturals
Greg's idea of what a natural can accomplish is abysmal; such low standards kill young lifters' drive and dreams
Insulting obese people into action can work; NH is not opposed to the practice if it yields results
Drama and gossip content is endless and easy to produce, which is why drama channels do so well, but it has no real value

Buff Dudes: experience 10 (20-30 combined years of lifting through injuries, bulks and kids), dogmatism 10, humor 10, production 10, drama-free; but programming 3, empathy 4 because they feel like actors, and past thumbnails used sexualised female images for clicks
Most fitness channels are good for novices, worse for intermediates and fairly useless for advanced lifters, because they target novices
Sean Nalewanyj scored 148.5/200: programming emphasised because it is the way for naturals, integrity 9, usefulness 9, science 8 because he never weaponises studies; humor 3 and very formulaic titles
Plate presses will not build a big chest
Creators who try to relate to the everyday person suffer the curse of the ordinary: they lose entertainment value

Omar Isuf scored 143/200: a pioneer of programming on YouTube who learned from powerlifters, character 10, empathy 9; but content recycling 1 (around 25 overhead press videos) and dogmatically skewed toward powerlifting
A coach who plateaus in aesthetics may start believing that is the natural limit and pass the belief on to viewers
Omar's physique, like NH's, is nothing special and achievable by anyone
Creatine is the least damaging supplement to sell

Ryan Humiston scored 100/200: programming 3 (attacks time-tested progressive overload), integrity 2 (a character playing a role), usefulness 3.5; production 10, conciseness 10 and physique 10 but enhanced
Progressive overload is true and time-tested; attacking it to reinvent the wheel is damaging
Anything works for novices, so a channel working for noobs proves little; for intermediates bad advice can cause regression
Bad advice inadvertently black-pills people: they follow it, see no results and conclude they have bad genetics
Strong personalities attract weak personalities who become fanboys and copy blindly instead of becoming doers
Creators who belittle viewers in a 'daddy' style tap into men who grew up without fathers and create stunted individuals
Thumbnails built on fear and anxiety ('big mistake', 'do this') exist to force clicks
Putting one's own face and body on thumbnails feeds parasocial relationships
